```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(knitr)

liquor <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
) |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
```

## ARIMA vs. ETS

### 2.1 The Data

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail Sales: Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
    subtitle = "Not seasonally adjusted, Jan 1992 - Dec 2019",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot: Log Liquor Store Sales",
       x = "Month", y = "log(Sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Sales are trending up from 1992-2019. The holidays show a peak each year (December) with January to February being the lowest. The seasonal swing is growing with the level of sales but displays stability when logged, so I would apply log of sales.

### 2.2 Fit Both Models

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_fit.rds")

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

ARIMA chose ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] w/ drift.  Series was not differenced (d = 0) but seasonally differenced one time (D = 1), so each month is compared to the same month from a year earlier. ETS chose ETS(A,A,A): additive errors, additive trend, and additive seasonality. Since the model is on log of sales, additive seasonality implies that the seasonalswings are a constant % of the level.

```{r}
#| echo: false
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

Residuals are centered at 0 and normal, but a few ACF spikes (ie. lag 24) are outside the bounds. Ljung-Box test rejects white noise (p<0.05), so some of the seasonal features are left over. The horse race will show us whether or not that hurts our forecast.

## VAR vs. BVAR

### 4.1 Data

120 forecasts pervariable (240 quarters minus the 120-quarter training sample). First forecast is 1990 Q1 and the last 2019 Q4.

### 4.2 OLS VARs

VAR1 beats VAR4 for 7/8 variables (all except for inflation which nearly tied). VAR4 has 264 coefficients vs 72 for VAR1. It is overfitting noise from the training sample which adds some estimation error to its forecasts.

### 4.3 BVAR

```{r}
#| echo: false
readRDS("results/var_results.rds") |> kable(digits = 3)
var_dm <- readRDS("results/var_dm.rds")
var_dm$gdp
var_dm$inv
```

BVAR4 with lambda = 0.3 beats the OLS VAR4 for all of the variables. Same variables and lags so the gain comes solely from the Minnesota prior decreasing the 264 coefficients towards zero (cuts estimation error).

Against the VAR1, the BVAR wins for 3 of the variables (investment, inflation and 10-year yield) and loses for the 5.

w/ lambda = 0.05, RMSEs get worse for most variables (employment and inflation by a relatively great amount) and only improve for the fed. funds rate. That's way too much shrinkage (the coefficients are pushed so close to zero that the model loses real function). The winners RMSE in this table would not be a fair estimate of future accuracy since we picked it once we saw  the results on this same sample.

DM tests (VAR4 vs. BVAR lambda = 0.3): GDP growth DM = 2.14, p = 0.035, so the BVAR is more accurate. Investment growth w/ DM = 1.63, p = 0.107 (not significant). So some of the RMSE gaps in the table could be noise.

## Factor Model

### 5.1–5.2 Data and Factors

```{r}
#| echo: false
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))
transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code), "1" = x, "2" = d(x), "3" = d(d(x)), "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)), "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))), "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}
fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]

F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))
tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) + geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal()

sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

INDPRO (code 5): monthly growth rate. PAYEMS (code 5): monthly growth rate. CPIAUCSL (code 6): change in the monthly inflation rate. FEDFUNDS (code 2): first differenced. Int rates are already in % and can be near zero, so logs don't make sense; a simple difference makes them stationary.

The first 3 factors explain 29.5% of the variation in the 121 series (15.0%, 7.4%, 7.1%).

Factor 1 has most correlation w/ payroll employment, industrial production, and manufacturing hours/employment, so it's a real activity factor; it drops sharply in recessions (1974–75, 1980–82, 2008–09). Factor 2 is most correlated w/ CPI and PCE, so it's an nflation factor.

### 5.3 IP Horse Race

```{r}
#| echo: false
readRDS("results/ip_rmse.rds")
```

RMSEs 0.617 for the AR1 and 0.589 w/ factors. Estimating the factors once on the full sample would be dishonest because each forecast would use data from after the forecast origin (biased), making the factor model look better than it could be in real time.

### 5.4 Direct Forecast of Inflation

```{r}
#| echo: false
readRDS("results/cpi_race.rds") |> kable(digits = 3)
```

Yes, addding in factors cuts the RMSE of 12 month CPI inflation forecasts (from 2.11 to 1.89, about a 10.2% reduction). MAE drops from 1.58 to 1.35. The DM p-value is 0.0004 which means the improvement is statistically significant.
